results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included, after reasonable exclusion of other disorders.

output.summary: No cohort data link human herpesvirus 7 to anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis; published cohort evidence identifies HSV encephalitis as an established trigger and describes a non-specific infectious-like prodrome in most patients.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Serum anti-GluN1 positive (1:64); sodium 134 mEq/L; thyroid function and thyroid antibodies negative; toxicology negative
action_criteria.label: Obtain the reviewed serum work-up, including a cell-based IgG anti-GluN1 assay that must be interpreted with CSF rather than alone
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, toxic and infective causes of new seizures and gives the serum anti-GluN1 result, which is read with the CSF assay.

action_criteria.label: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI to exclude HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination; a normal MRI does not exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis
action_criteria.rationale: New seizures with GCS 9 need imaging before LP to exclude HSV encephalitis and structural lesions; MRI does not confirm the diagnosis.

action_criteria.rationale: The CSF cell-based anti-GluN1 assay is decisive even when cells, protein and oligoclonal bands are normal, and the HSV PCR excludes HSV encephalitis.

action_criteria.rationale: Tumors are rare in young men with anti-NMDAR encephalitis, but a testicular germ-cell tumor is the one to look for, and its removal would be part of first-line treatment.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1 to 2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.

Do not attribute the encephalitis to HHV-7 or treat it with antivirals alone: HHV-7 DNA in a CSF without pleocytosis is of uncertain significance, and the CSF anti-GluN1 antibody explains the illness.
required_recommendations: Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, with hydration and without NSAIDs, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).
Scrotal ultrasound shows no tumor; no further tumor imaging is needed unless the course is atypical or refractory.
Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide, with a benzodiazepine for any seizure lasting over 5 minutes; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.

Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for GCS 9, post-ictal hypoventilation with desaturation to 71% and recurrent seizures, with airway assessment (intubation if consciousness or ventilation worsens) and cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioral management.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

key_clinical_evidence: Days after a gastrointestinal prodrome, new generalized and focal seizures, cognitive slowing, orofacial dyskinesias and chorea, reduced consciousness (GCS 9) and autonomic instability: five of the six Graus 2016 groups.

CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titer 1:128) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016) despite a CSF without pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands; serum positive 1:64 is read with the CSF.

MRI shows bilateral hippocampal FLAIR signal (left greater than right) without restricted diffusion or hemorrhage; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds, and the negative CSF HSV PCR excludes HSV encephalitis.
EEG shows extreme delta brush and a left frontotemporal seizure; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
HHV-7 DNA in a non-inflammatory CSF is of uncertain significance and does not displace the antibody diagnosis.
Scrotal ultrasound shows no tumor; earlier immunotherapy is associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability and encephalopathy that persists between seizures are red flags for autoimmune encephalitis and require CSF antibody testing.
red_herrings.data_point: Two generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a previously healthy 19-year-old after a presumed stomach virus.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on new-onset epilepsy or provoked seizures with post-ictal confusion.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis. At 134 mEq/L it does not cause seizures.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a metabolic cause of the seizures instead of the neurological work-up.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome needs antipsychotic exposure and a markedly raised CK; this mild rise reflects seizures and dyskinesias and does not change management.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raises concern for neuroleptic malignant syndrome or rhabdomyolysis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: HHV-7 DNA in a CSF without pleocytosis or intrathecal synthesis is of uncertain significance; the CSF anti-GluN1 antibody explains the illness and immunotherapy is needed.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent to diagnose HHV-7 encephalitis and stop at an antiviral plan.

patient.history_present_illness: This 19-year-old right-handed male university student was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after his roommate witnessed two generalized tonic-clonic seizures over a 48-hour period. According to the roommate and the patient's parents who were contacted by phone, the patient had been complaining of abdominal pain and nausea approximately four days prior to presentation. Two days before admission, he developed a low-grade temperature of 37.5 degrees Celsius, vomited once, and appeared unusually fatigued but attributed his symptoms to a stomach virus. He missed two days of classes, which was unusual for him. The following day, his roommate heard rhythmic banging sounds from the patient's bed at approximately 2 AM and found him having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure with limb stiffening, rhythmic jerking, and urinary incontinence, lasting approximately two minutes. The patient was drowsy and confused afterward but appeared to recover over several hours, though he remained uncharacteristically quiet and had difficulty following conversations. His roommate noted that he seemed 'spaced out' and was making unusual repetitive lip-smacking movements that were not present previously. The next morning, approximately 22 hours after the first event, the patient had a second generalized seizure witnessed by his roommate, this time lasting nearly three minutes with post-ictal confusion lasting over an hour. Emergency medical services were called. The paramedics administered intravenous midazolam 5 mg for seizure management en route. On arrival, the patient was somnolent with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 9, displayed intermittent orofacial dyskinesias, and had markedly decreased oxygen saturation at 71% on room air with perioral cyanosis, which improved to 94% with supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula at 4 liters per minute. His parents reported that he had no prior seizure history, no psychiatric history, no recent head trauma, no recent travel to tick-endemic areas, and no known drug use. They noted he had a confirmed COVID-19 infection approximately 18 months ago with a mild course and full recovery, and that SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies were found positive on a subsequent check. His mother has autoimmune thyroiditis, and his maternal grandmother has rheumatoid arthritis.

neurological_exam.additional: Two brief episodes of generalized stiffening with tonic extension lasting approximately 30-40 seconds each witnessed in the emergency department, followed by post-ictal unresponsiveness. Orofacial dyskinesias with repetitive lip-smacking and jaw movements observed intermittently. Episodes of autonomic instability including transient tachycardia to 120 bpm and blood pressure fluctuations from 100/60 to 145/90 mmHg observed during the examination period. Perioral cyanosis noted during one tonic episode before supplemental oxygen applied.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements appear intact on oculocephalic reflex testing. Corneal reflexes present bilaterally. Facial sensation intact to nailbed pressure. Mild symmetric facial hypotonia noted. Gag reflex intact. Tongue midline. No overt cranial nerve palsies identified. No meningeal signs (Kernig and Brudzinski negative).

neurological_exam.mental_status: Somnolent, difficult to arouse. GCS 9 (E2 V3 M4). Opens eyes to painful stimuli. Verbalizations limited to incomprehensible sounds and occasional moaning. Does not follow commands. Unable to assess orientation, attention, or memory due to severely altered level of consciousness. During brief periods of relative alertness, displays purposeless agitation with repetitive vocalizations.

No decorticate or decerebrate posturing. Intermittent involuntary choreiform movements of bilateral upper extremities observed during examination.
